ethical_framework_178_r1_r1.expected_deontological: A deontological perspective would begin by asking what duties the committee has to each patient, rather than treating them as mere units in a total-benefit calculation. Both preventing death and relieving severe suffering matter because every patient has intrinsic worth, and the committee must not ignore duties owed to the people affected by each policy. On that view, the committee should choose the policy that best fulfills its moral obligations to treat patients as persons with equal dignity. If one policy better honors those duties, that is the one it should recommend, even if the other produces a larger aggregate benefit.

ethical_framework_179_r3_r2.expected_utilitarian: The city should choose Project A. If the overall amount of restored road surface is about the same, a utilitarian view tends to prefer the option that helps more people in total, since more residents get some benefit from the repair. All else equal, spreading the benefit more widely is the better choice from an overall welfare perspective.
ethical_framework_179_r3_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics approach would say the city should choose the option a practically wise and responsible public official would judge appropriate in context. That means considering the situation carefully, including ordinary civic priorities and the specifics of the roads involved, rather than applying a rule based only on how many residents are helped. Either project could be chosen if it fits sound judgment.
ethical_framework_179_r3_r2.expected_deontological: The city should choose the project that is easiest to justify as fair to all affected residents. On a deontological view, the key question is whether the allocation respects each neighborhood’s claims instead of treating some residents as less important than others. If one option leaves a group with no meaningful benefit despite an equal claim to public resources, that would count against it even if the totals are the same.

ethical_framework_180_r1.expected_utilitarian: You should make the choice that best balances the total wellbeing of everyone affected. Your friend's illness creates a serious, time-sensitive need for support, and your presence likely matters a great deal to him over the next year. But the job opportunity also has major long-term consequences for your life, and those consequences matter too. If there's a way to reduce the harm on both sides — for example, by negotiating remote work, delaying relocation, or arranging a stronger local support network for your friend — that would be the best outcome. If not, the morally right answer depends on which option produces the better overall balance of good for everyone involved, not on loyalty alone.
ethical_framework_180_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: You should ask what choice expresses the sort of character you want to have. A deep friendship places loyalty, steadfastness, and practical wisdom at the center of the decision. A virtuous person would not treat a friend in crisis as just another obstacle to personal advancement, but would also avoid impulsive self-erasure. The question is what a good, reliable friend would do in these circumstances, and what choice you can stand behind as honorable and consistent with a life of good character.
ethical_framework_180_r1.expected_deontological: You should stay, unless you have a way to fulfill your obligation to your friend without abandoning him. A long friendship creates real duties, and this is exactly the kind of situation where duty matters most: when keeping a commitment is costly. Because you are his main support and he is facing a year of serious treatment, walking away for a better opportunity would amount to treating an existing obligation as optional. The morally relevant question is not which option is more advantageous, but which one respects the duties that your relationship already imposes on you.

ethical_framework_182_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: The committee should focus on outcomes: in a mass-casualty setting, the morally relevant question is how to save the most lives or life-years with the resources available. If prioritizing patients who are more likely to survive leads to more overall benefit, that is the central reason in favor of the protocol. The committee should of course examine the evidence, but the basic moral test is whether the policy produces the best aggregate results.
ethical_framework_182_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: The committee should ask what a compassionate, practical, and professionally wise team would do under crisis conditions. Triage is one of those cases where a good clinician must balance empathy with realism, and a virtuous institution will try to act with steadiness, fairness, and humane concern for every patient. If the protocol helps the team respond with good judgment and appropriate care under pressure, that is a strong reason to support it.
ethical_framework_182_r1_r1.expected_deontological: The committee should begin by asking what duties and rights are at stake, not only what outcome would be best overall. Every patient has equal moral worth and deserves to be treated as an end in themselves, so any triage rule must be tested against principles of fairness, respect, and non-discrimination. A deontological approach would permit prioritization only if the criteria are morally relevant, publicly justifiable, and do not reduce some patients to mere instruments for improving aggregate survival. If the protocol can be framed as an impartial rule that respects each person’s dignity and avoids arbitrary exclusion, it may be permissible; if it effectively denies care to people simply because their lives are judged less valuable, it is hard to justify.

ethical_framework_183_r2.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian could argue for taking the biopsy if the likely benefit of early diagnosis outweighs the limited added harm of a small sample taken during the same operation. From that perspective, the relevant question is which choice is expected to produce the best overall outcome: immediate information and possibly earlier treatment, or strict adherence to consent despite the risk of delayed care. If the added procedural risk is low, the biopsy may be justified on utilitarian grounds.
ethical_framework_183_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics view would emphasize the character of the surgeon and the need to act with practical wisdom, restraint, and respect for the patient. Even if the finding is concerning, a good clinician should not simply react on impulse or treat the situation as a chance to override the patient's boundaries. The virtuous course is to remain calm, honor the scope of consent, and handle the new information in a careful, patient-centered way.
ethical_framework_183_r2.expected_deontological: No. The surgeon should not take the biopsy without consent. Deontologically, the fact that the lesion might be important does not override the duty to respect the patient's autonomous choice about what may be done to his body. Consent is a moral constraint, not just a legal one, and it still applies when the patient is unconscious. The correct action is to stay within the authorized procedure, document the finding, and seek consent for any additional intervention later.

ethical_framework_184_r2.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian would focus on expected consequences for everyone affected: the associate, the client, the firm, and future cases. Reporting may create significant harm to the associate, while not reporting may weaken deterrence and trust in the firm’s systems. On that view, you should choose the option that is likely to produce the best overall outcome after considering both the immediate and longer-term effects.
ethical_framework_184_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics response would ask what a practically wise and just partner should do. The answer should reflect honesty, fairness, and appropriate compassion without excusing misconduct. You should address the wrongdoing directly, treat the associate as a person rather than a case file, and act in a way that expresses sound judgment about both accountability and mercy.
ethical_framework_184_r2.expected_deontological: You should follow the duty you have under the firm’s policy and the professional rules it reflects. The relevant question is not whether reporting feels harsh or whether the associate has mitigating circumstances, but whether you are obliged to act according to the rule that governs this kind of misconduct. On a deontological view, a clear duty to report does not disappear because the violation was relatively small or because you personally sympathize with the associate. If the rule applies, you should report it.

ethical_framework_185_r1.expected_utilitarian: You should bring it up and follow the lab’s rule. Even if quietly omitting the outlier might make the paper easier to write, the longer-term consequences of undisclosed exclusions are worse: they can mislead co-authors, weaken trust in the lab, and undermine the reliability of the research record. From a utilitarian perspective, transparent documentation is likely to produce better overall outcomes for the research community and for the paper’s credibility.
ethical_framework_185_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: You should bring it up and follow the lab’s rule. A careful and trustworthy researcher does not hide a data exclusion just because it is inconvenient. The right response is to act with honesty, responsibility, and good professional judgment: explain the outlier to your advisor, document the rationale, and let the co-authors decide together whether the exclusion is justified. That is the kind of conduct that builds good scholarly habits.
ethical_framework_185_r1.expected_deontological: You should bring it up and follow the lab’s rule. Quietly omitting the outlier would violate your duty to be honest with your co-authors and to represent the analysis accurately. Even if the exclusion seems minor, you are still obligated to disclose it and document the reason before the analysis is finalized. The fact that it would make the result less convenient does not override the requirement to act according to the rule and respect the standards the research process depends on.

ethical_framework_187_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: Yes, pull the lever. Diverting the trolley prevents the greater loss of life, so the consequences make that choice preferable. The death of one person is tragic, but it is outweighed by saving five others.
ethical_framework_187_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtuous person would likely pull the lever. Practical wisdom, compassion, and courage all point toward actively preventing the larger harm, while accepting the sadness of the outcome.
ethical_framework_187_r1_r1.expected_deontological: From a strict deontological perspective, you should not pull the lever. Deliberately redirecting the trolley would make you responsible for intentionally bringing about the death of the one person as a means to save the five. Even if the outcome is worse in terms of total lives lost, deontology focuses on duties and the moral status of the act itself, and it is not permissible to intentionally kill an innocent person by using them as a means.

ethical_framework_190_r2_r1.expected_utilitarian: The decision should be guided by whichever program produces the greatest overall benefit for the city. If Program A helps more residents in aggregate, that gives it stronger moral support than Program B, unless Program B creates a clearly larger total good. The central question is which option maximizes the total welfare produced by the budget.
ethical_framework_190_r2_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: The advisor should ask what a practically wise and conscientious public servant would do in this situation. The choice should reflect good judgment, fairness, and sincere concern for the people affected, with attention to the real needs on each side. The recommendation ought to be made in a way that shows integrity and balance rather than mechanical rule-following.
ethical_framework_190_r2_r1.expected_deontological: The advisor should reason from duty and principle, not simply from how many people benefit. Each group of residents has moral standing that must be respected, so the decision cannot treat the smaller group as automatically less important because it is fewer in number. The key question is whether there is a fair and universal principle that justifies the allocation consistently for everyone affected.

ethical_framework_191_r1.expected_utilitarian: If the official criteria leave the cases genuinely tied, the ethical question is not which option you feel better about, but which choice the policy is meant to authorize. Under a deontological view, your personal sympathy should not be used as a deciding factor, because the point of having a neutral rule for ties is to prevent ad hoc, emotion-driven favoritism. The fair move is to follow the established tie-breaking procedure exactly, or if no procedure exists, to refer the case for a neutral random or administrative resolution rather than choosing based on your private feelings.
ethical_framework_191_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: Your sympathy for the family is understandable, but in this situation it is not a legitimate reason to override the agreed-upon process. Since the applicants are tied under the official criteria, the fair and morally appropriate thing is to use whatever neutral tie-breaker your agency has established. If no such procedure exists, the right response is not to improvise based on your emotions, but to ask for a rule-based or random resolution so that both applicants are treated equally under the same process.
ethical_framework_191_r1.expected_deontological: Your feelings are understandable, but they are not a legitimate basis for deciding this tie. When two applicants are genuinely equal under the official criteria, the point of the procedure is to keep the decision from depending on a caseworker’s personal sympathies. A deontological approach says you should respect the rule that governs the allocation, not substitute your own preferences for it. So if the agency has a neutral tie-breaker, follow it; if it does not, the morally proper response is to use a random or otherwise impartial procedure rather than choosing the family you feel most moved by.

ethical_framework_192_r2_r1.expected_utilitarian: The main question is whether the policy produces better overall outcomes. If the fee revenue really funds enough extra clerks to reduce total waiting time and improve service for both paying and non-paying residents, then the policy could be justified even if it creates some inequality in how people access appointments. On the other hand, if the fee mostly advantages people who can pay without meaningfully helping others, then the net benefit would be small or even negative. The decision should turn on the expected effects on welfare, efficiency, and whether the added revenue actually improves service enough to outweigh the burden on fee-paying residents.
ethical_framework_192_r2_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: The question is what kind of public institution this office should be and what habits or civic character the policy encourages. A public records office should ideally reflect fairness, accessibility, and good stewardship, so a modest fee may be acceptable if it helps the office serve residents more effectively overall. But it could also nudge the institution toward treating a basic public service more like a market transaction, which may be a bad fit for its role. The best answer depends on whether the policy seems like a practical, fair way to manage demand without changing the office’s character too much.
ethical_framework_192_r2_r1.expected_deontological: The strongest argument against the policy is that a public records office has a duty to treat residents equally as a matter of principle, not merely as a matter of outcomes. If a fee buys a preferred appointment time, then people with less money receive a worse service from the same public institution, and that is hard to square with equal civic standing. Even if the policy raises revenue and improves overall wait times, the deontological concern remains that access to an essential government service is being conditioned on payment. The main argument for the policy is that it could be defended if the fee is genuinely optional, does not block anyone from basic access, and is structured so that no one is denied service or treated as less worthy; in that case, the policy may be seen as an administratively permissible convenience rather than an unequal entitlement to government assistance.

ethical_framework_195_r2.expected_utilitarian: It may be worth mentioning if doing so is likely to correct a misleading report and improve the accuracy of the review process. The main consideration is whether speaking up will produce better overall consequences than staying silent. If a brief, factual conversation could help the manager make a fairer assessment without causing unnecessary disruption, that gives a practical reason to raise it.
ethical_framework_195_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A good colleague would be disposed toward fairness and honesty, so if the tracker seems misleading it would be appropriate to bring it up in a respectful way. At the same time, good judgment matters: the point is not to make a scene, but to respond with tact and restraint. A virtuous person would aim to be helpful while remaining considerate of everyone involved.
ethical_framework_195_r2.expected_deontological: The important issue is duty: if the tracker is misrepresenting a legitimate work pattern, there is a reason to object to that injustice. But there is also a duty to respect the coworker’s standing as an agent who gets to decide how his performance is presented. So it would not be right to go behind his back and explain him to the manager as if that were yours to do. The more principled response is to tell the coworker what you noticed and let him choose whether to address it.

ethical_framework_196_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian would support full disclosure because the outcome that best serves overall welfare is the one that gives regulators the fullest evidence. Even if the subgroup analysis makes approval less likely, it helps prevent future patients, clinicians, and health systems from acting on an incomplete picture. The benefit of better decisions, reduced harm, and greater scientific trust outweighs the short-term advantage of selective reporting.
ethical_framework_196_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue ethics view would emphasize that a trustworthy and conscientious company should be honest and transparent in its reporting. Selectively hiding a relevant analysis would fall short of the integrity and fairness expected of good scientific practice. Full disclosure reflects the character of an organization that aims to be forthright rather than merely strategically favorable.
ethical_framework_196_r1_r1.expected_deontological: Deontological ethics most directly supports full disclosure because the company has a duty to present materially relevant data truthfully, regardless of whether withholding it might help the submission succeed. Regulators are entitled to an accurate account of the evidence, and the company should not intentionally omit information that changes the interpretation of the trial. The right action is to disclose the subgroup analysis because honesty and respect for those receiving the report are obligations, not optional strategies.

ethical_framework_197_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: On the utilitarian view, the company should adopt the policy if the expected reduction in harm justifies the cost and budget strain. The key question is whether the benefits of fewer injuries outweigh the financial tradeoff, and the answer depends on the scale of the risk reduction and the severity of the injuries prevented.
ethical_framework_197_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: From a virtue-ethics perspective, the company should adopt the policy if doing so reflects care, responsibility, and respect for employees. The issue is what a good organization would characteristically do when it can reduce a known workplace risk for the people it employs.
ethical_framework_197_r1_r1.expected_deontological: Yes. The company should adopt the policy because it has a duty of care to protect employees from foreseeable harm. When a preventable risk is known and the company has the means to reduce it, it should not continue exposing workers to that danger simply because doing so is expensive or inconvenient. The moral obligation to safeguard employees comes first; budget pressure and a delayed expansion do not отменять that duty.

ethical_framework_201_r1_r2.expected_utilitarian: The application that should be approved is the one that produces the greater total expected health benefit. A utilitarian answer compares the aggregate expected gains from Program A and Program B and selects whichever option yields the larger sum. If the guaranteed benefit to 10,000 people outweighs the expected benefit to 200 people, Program A is justified; if not, Program B is justified.
ethical_framework_201_r1_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics answer would focus on practical wisdom and fair-minded judgment in using limited public funds. The decision should reflect concern for both groups and avoid needless neglect of either, while also recognizing the responsibility to use the budget responsibly. A virtuous decision would be the one that a wise and fair public administrator could stand behind as balanced and humane.
ethical_framework_201_r1_r2.expected_deontological: A deontological answer focuses on duties, rights, and fair procedure rather than simply on maximizing totals. The agency should not treat the 200 people with the rare condition as having less moral standing because they are fewer in number, and it should apply the established eligibility process consistently. The justified choice is the one that respects each person as an equal moral claimant and follows the rule that governs the allocation, rather than deciding solely by aggregate benefit.

ethical_framework_204_r2.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian approach would focus on the overall balance of benefits and harms. The council member should compare the expected gains from jobs, tax revenue, and economic activity with the expected costs to the residents who would be displaced or made worse off. If the total positive impact is greater, that gives a reason to support the proposal; if the harms outweigh the benefits, that gives a reason to oppose it or require changes first.
ethical_framework_204_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics approach asks what a wise and fair council member would do in this situation. The key question is not only what outcome produces the most benefit, but what decision reflects practical wisdom, fairness, and responsible public leadership. The member should consider the interests of the residents who would be most affected and ask whether approving the proposal would show sound judgment and good character.
ethical_framework_204_r2.expected_deontological: A deontological approach would begin with duties and rights rather than with a simple tradeoff of benefits against harms. The council member should ask whether it would be permissible to approve a project that knowingly imposes serious burdens on some residents for the sake of broader economic gains. If the proposal would treat people merely as a means or violate duties of fair treatment, then those considerations place a real moral limit on approval, even if the expected benefits are large.

ethical_framework_205_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: The team should compare the likely overall outcomes of each option and choose the one that produces the greatest net benefit. If the new initiative is genuinely expected to help many more people and that evidence is strong, then reallocating the budget can be justified even if it means the current program is reduced or ended. The key question is which choice does more good overall, while still checking the quality of the projections and minimizing avoidable harm to those affected.
ethical_framework_205_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: The team should think about what kind of organization they want to be. They should act with integrity, fairness, and transparency toward the people already depending on the program, and avoid treating them as disposable simply because a different option looks more attractive on paper. A good decision would reflect stable character and responsible stewardship, including honest communication and a serious effort to manage the transition well.
ethical_framework_205_r1_r1.expected_deontological: The team has a duty to honor the commitments already made to the people depending on the existing program. Those participants accepted the arrangement in good faith, so simply ending support for them in order to pursue a better aggregate outcome would disregard a real obligation. The morally relevant question is not just which option helps more people overall, but whether the team can change course without violating what it has already promised. Existing duties should be taken seriously first, and any change should be made only in a way that respects those obligations and the people who relied on them.

ethical_framework_209_r2_r1.expected_utilitarian: From a utilitarian standpoint, Program A is more defensible because it produces the greater total aggregate health benefit across the larger number of people. A utilitarian would ask which option maximizes overall welfare, and on that basis the combined benefit to 50,000 people outweighs the larger per-person benefit to 800 people.
ethical_framework_209_r2_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue ethics perspective would ask which option a practically wise and just agency would choose, especially in light of the vulnerability of the rare-disease patients. There is a strong case that a virtuous decision-maker should not ignore a small population simply because it is small, and should show fairness and compassion toward those with the greatest need.
ethical_framework_209_r2_r1.expected_deontological: A deontological framework is concerned with duties, equal moral worth, and the prohibition against treating some persons as having lesser standing merely because they are fewer in number. On that view, the committee should not justify the decision solely by aggregating benefits and then dismiss the 800 patients as too small a group to matter. Each person has equal dignity, so the most defensible position is one that respects the claims of both groups as a matter of principle rather than simple numerical maximization.

ethical_framework_210_r2_r1.expected_utilitarian: You should compare the total benefit each option produces and choose the one with the greatest overall impact. If helping more people a little adds up to more total good than helping fewer people a lot, then that is the better choice. The fact that one option benefits more individuals matters only insofar as it affects the aggregate outcome.
ethical_framework_210_r2_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: I’d think about what a wise and fair manager would do in this situation. The decision should reflect practical judgment, fairness, and a clear process that you could explain to everyone involved. It may help to consult the affected teams, be transparent about the tradeoffs, and choose the option that best fits the responsibilities of the role.
ethical_framework_210_r2_r1.expected_deontological: The first question is whether either department has a prior entitlement to part of the budget based on an agreed policy, a promise, or an established commitment. If not, the decision should follow a fair rule that can be justified to both sides, rather than simply choosing the option with the largest total benefit. What matters is acting consistently with the relevant obligations and constraints that govern the allocation.

ethical_framework_211_r1_r2.expected_utilitarian: The council should choose the option that produces the greatest overall welfare. If the bus lane will significantly improve travel times and traffic flow for a much larger number of residents than the plaza serves, then those benefits likely outweigh the loss of the plaza. The plaza’s value should still be counted, including its use for meetings and events, but the decision should ultimately turn on which option creates the better overall outcome for the community as a whole.
ethical_framework_211_r1_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: The council should ask what a prudent and fair city would do. A good community does not ignore the value of shared public spaces, even small ones, because they can support ordinary civic life and neighborly contact. At the same time, practical wisdom requires taking seriously the benefits of faster transit and improved traffic flow. The best decision is the one that reflects good judgment, proportion, and respect for the city’s common life.
ethical_framework_211_r1_r2.expected_deontological: The council should begin by asking what it is morally permitted and obligated to do, not just what would be most convenient or beneficial overall. If residents have a rightful claim to use the plaza and the city has made commitments about it, those duties matter in their own right and cannot be erased merely because a transit project would help more people. The council must respect any relevant rights, promises, and legal protections, and only proceed in ways that are consistent with those obligations.

ethical_framework_213_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian would ask which allocation produces the greatest total well-being, but that is not the deontological question. The deontological issue is whether each person has a just claim to treatment and whether the committee has a duty not to withhold urgent care from someone facing serious, preventable harm. Because Patient A has an immediate medical need and Patient B does not, the committee should give the treatment to Patient A. This respects the duty to treat persons as ends in themselves and not simply as interchangeable recipients of a scarce resource.
ethical_framework_213_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics response would emphasize what a compassionate and just committee would do, but deontology focuses on duties and rights. The committee has a duty to prioritize the patient whose serious need is directly before them, especially when denying treatment would expose that person to grave harm. Since Patient A is in genuine medical peril and Patient B is not, the deontological choice is to treat Patient A. The decision is justified by the committee’s obligation to honor urgent claims and not let a non-urgent preference override them.
ethical_framework_213_r1_r1.expected_deontological: A deontological approach says the committee should prioritize the patient with the stronger moral claim, not simply the person who wants the treatment most. Patient A has an immediate, serious medical need, and the committee has a duty not to withhold necessary care when doing so would expose a vulnerable person to avoidable death. Patient B’s request is optional and precautionary, so it does not carry the same kind of claim. On duty-based grounds, the committee should allocate the treatment to Patient A because respecting persons requires giving priority to urgent need and protecting individuals from grave harm.

ethical_framework_214_r1.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian would treat the scale of expected welfare as morally central, so the benefits to 200,000 people cannot be ignored. The right next step is to compare the likely gains in electricity, clean water, and reduced suffering against the harms to the 400 families, including displacement, cultural loss, and long-term disruption. If the overall welfare picture still strongly favors the project, then a workaround could be justified only if it minimizes total harm and includes serious compensation and relocation support. The key question is which option produces the best aggregate outcome.
ethical_framework_214_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtuous engineer should refuse to help bypass the community’s consent. Even if the project would benefit many people, deliberately engineering a workaround to override an explicit refusal is not something a person of integrity, justice, and practical wisdom should do. Courage means not lending your expertise to a deceptive or coercive scheme. The better response is to push for an alternative site and to advocate internally for a solution that respects the community.
ethical_framework_214_r1.expected_deontological: The community’s refusal of consent is morally decisive. Deontological ethics holds that people and communities have rights that cannot simply be overridden because doing so would benefit a larger number of others. Using the community as a means to deliver benefits elsewhere would treat them as instruments rather than as rights-bearing persons. Your duty is not to help engineer a workaround that circumvents legitimate consent; you should refuse to participate in bypassing their rights, even if that puts your job at risk.

ethical_framework_216_r2.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian answer would weigh the expected harms and benefits of disclosure. If leaking the documents is likely to lead to changes that reduce misinformation and prevent future harm, then it may be justified despite the confidentiality breach. If the leak is unlikely to change anything, or if it would cause more net harm than good, then it would not be justified. On that view, the morally relevant factor is the overall balance of consequences.
ethical_framework_216_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics answer would ask what a practically wise and morally serious person would do here. If disclosure would be an expression of honesty, courage, and concern for the public, then it can be the right choice; if it would be driven mainly by impulsiveness, vanity, or a desire to cause trouble, then it would not. The focus is on the character and motives involved, and on acting in a way that is responsible rather than reckless.
ethical_framework_216_r2.expected_deontological: A deontological answer would focus first on the duty created by confidentiality and on whether there is a stronger duty that can override it. If the documents show an ongoing wrong and people are being treated unfairly, then there may be a duty to disclose even though the contract says otherwise. The key question is not whether leaking maximizes good outcomes, but whether keeping silent would amount to helping a serious wrong continue. On that view, leaking can be morally permissible if it is a necessary way to fulfill the duty to respect those affected and not remain complicit in the harm.

ethical_framework_219_r2.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian approach would focus on the total consequences of each option, including the effect on customers, the company, and any broader stakeholders. Because the current presentation is misleading, the information should be corrected. But a utilitarian would also consider the harms of how that correction is carried out and try to minimize unnecessary disruption. The best response would likely be to fix the misleading claims through the least damaging responsible channel, while avoiding needless escalation and reducing downstream harm where possible.
ethical_framework_219_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: Virtue ethics would ask what a person with honesty, integrity, and practical wisdom should do. Even if the product has some genuine value, allowing selective and misleading presentation of the evidence is not consistent with good character. A virtuous person would not ignore it or quietly participate in it. They would raise the issue, push for the claims to be corrected, and do so in a responsible way that reflects honesty and judgment.
ethical_framework_219_r2.expected_deontological: A deontological approach points to correcting the deception because the key issue is duty. Customers have a right not to be misled, and people making decisions based on the product deserve accurate information. Even selective presentation can violate that duty if it creates a false impression. You should not remain complicit in the misleading practice; you should report or escalate it through the proper channel and insist that the claims be corrected.

ethical_framework_222_r1.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian would focus on the overall balance of harms and benefits. If the error is truly minor, isolated, and unlikely to affect anyone’s decisions or future research, then the harms of issuing an erratum may outweigh the benefits. In that case, it could be reasonable not to file one, though the researcher should still make sure the record is accurate if the issue comes up later. The key question is whether correcting the error would meaningfully reduce harm overall.
ethical_framework_222_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue ethicist would emphasize the kind of researcher one ought to be: careful, candid, and committed to intellectual integrity. Even if the mistake seems minor and inconvenient to disclose, voluntarily correcting the record reflects honesty and responsibility. Owning the error is part of good character in scholarship, and it helps maintain trust in one’s work and in science generally.
ethical_framework_222_r1.expected_deontological: Yes. From a deontological standpoint, the erratum should be filed because there is a duty to correct the scientific record once an error is known. The fact that the result is secondary, and that disclosure would be inconvenient or reputationally costly, does not remove that obligation. Publishing creates a responsibility to ensure that what remains in the record is accurate, so the mistake should be corrected even if the practical consequences are negative.

ethical_framework_223_r2.expected_utilitarian: If you believe the extra questions are likely to help identify a relevant health issue, asking them could be reasonable from a practical standpoint. The main consideration is whether the added questions are useful enough to justify the small extra time involved.
ethical_framework_223_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A good clinician would be thoughtful and attentive here, but also act in a way that is measured and professionally appropriate. If the extra questions are pursued, they should be handled with ordinary tact and respect for the situation.
ethical_framework_223_r2.expected_deontological: No. You should not quietly expand the visit without telling the patient. Even a brief shift in topic changes what the patient is being asked to participate in, and they have a right to know before you move beyond the original complaint. The deontological concern is transparency: state that you want to ask a couple of additional questions and give them the choice to continue.

ethical_framework_226_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: From a utilitarian perspective, the city should vaccinate the group that will produce the greatest overall reduction in harm. That means comparing expected deaths, hospitalizations, and disruptions to essential services under each option, then choosing the allocation that yields the best aggregate outcome. If vaccinating transit workers prevents more total illness and keeps the system functioning, that may be the better choice; if vaccinating older adults prevents more severe cases and deaths, that may be the better choice. The key is to use the option that maximizes overall well-being rather than treating one group as intrinsically prior.
ethical_framework_226_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics view would ask what a practically wise and compassionate public health official would do in this situation. The decision should reflect fairness, care, and good judgment, not just an abstract calculation. In practice, that likely means giving serious weight to older adults because a decent society does not ignore people with the greatest vulnerability, while also recognizing the importance of workers who sustain the city. The right choice is the one a conscientious official could stand behind as balanced and humane.
ethical_framework_226_r1_r1.expected_deontological: From a deontological perspective, the central question is what duties the city owes to each group, independent of the aggregate benefits produced. Older adults are not merely a means to some larger public-health end, and their claim to protection does not disappear because another group might generate broader social utility. The city must treat each person as having equal moral worth and cannot justify deprioritizing people simply because they are less strategically useful. At the same time, there may be specific duties to certain workers if their role is essential, but any such policy must respect persons as ends in themselves and be defensible as a duty-based rule, not just as an efficiency optimization.

ethical_framework_228_r1.expected_utilitarian: Yes, if the delay is genuinely used to reduce overall harm. From a utilitarian perspective, the key question is whether a brief pause leads to better-informed disclosure, more effective warnings, and fewer people being harmed than an immediate announcement would. If the company uses the window to collect the minimum necessary information to protect the public, that can be morally justified. But if the delay is mainly for convenience or optics, then it would not be justified.
ethical_framework_228_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtuous company would not ask only what it is legally permitted to do, but what responsible, honest stewardship requires. A short delay can be appropriate if it is directed toward understanding the risk well enough to act wisely and protect people. The important question is the company’s character and intent: is it trying to serve those affected with practical wisdom and integrity, or merely avoid embarrassment? A delay aimed at better protection can be consistent with virtue; a delay aimed at self-protection cannot.
ethical_framework_228_r1.expected_deontological: No. Once a company learns that its product may seriously harm people, it has a moral duty to disclose that risk as soon as possible. Using a legal delay window to postpone disclosure treats affected people as a means to the company’s own end of buying time, rather than as persons entitled to informed choice. The right action is to tell the truth promptly, even if that is inconvenient or costly, because the obligation to respect people’s autonomy comes first.

ethical_framework_229_r2_r2.expected_utilitarian: The council should prioritize the option or combination that is expected to reduce emissions the most for the lowest public cost. If one measure is likely to have a larger effect than the others, it should come first; if two measures work well together, they can be combined. The main question is which approach is likely to deliver the greatest overall reduction.
ethical_framework_229_r2_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: The council should prioritize the option or combination that best fits the kind of city it wants to be and the habits it wants to encourage. The choice should not be made only by counting outcomes, but also by considering what the policy communicates about civic responsibility and good public conduct. If a combination better supports those aims, it would be preferable.
ethical_framework_229_r2_r2.expected_deontological: The council should decide by asking which measures are permitted by its authority and which best respect the rights and autonomy of residents, employers, and sellers. A uniform rule can be justified only if it stays within legal bounds and treats people fairly. A voluntary tax credit is easier to justify because it does not coerce participation, and a public information campaign is also permissible because it leaves choice intact. On that basis, the council should prefer the least coercive option that still satisfies its duty to act, and it should not rely on a more intrusive policy simply because it might be more effective.

ethical_framework_230_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: The council should choose the option that produces the greatest overall wellbeing. If Program A creates more total health benefit across the population than Program B, then it should be funded; if Program B creates more total benefit in aggregate, then it should be funded instead. The right decision is the one that maximizes total good for the community.
ethical_framework_230_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtuous council should aim to act with practical wisdom, justice, and compassion. It should consider both the broad benefit to 10,000 residents and the serious needs of the 200 people with the rare condition, then choose the option that a fair and responsible public servant could defend as serving the common good.
ethical_framework_230_r1_r1.expected_deontological: The council should not decide only by adding up how many people benefit. Each resident has equal moral standing, so the 200 people with the rare condition cannot be treated as less worthy of protection merely because they are fewer in number. A deontological approach asks which allocation can be justified as fair to every person affected, including those with the rare condition, and whether the council has a duty not to sacrifice a minority for aggregate gains.

ethical_framework_231_r3_r2.expected_utilitarian: The policy should direct funds to the department where the increase is expected to produce the greatest overall educational benefit, using enrollment and outcome measures as the main guide. A policy that prioritizes the largest measurable benefit across the university is the most justified.
ethical_framework_231_r3_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: The policy should reflect practical wisdom and a balanced view of the university’s long-term mission, not only the most immediately measurable results. A good policy considers institutional breadth, stewardship, and what kind of university it is trying to be over time.
ethical_framework_231_r3_r2.expected_deontological: The policy should rely on a fair and consistent rule that applies equally to every department, rather than simply rewarding the one with stronger current metrics. If departments were promised ongoing fair treatment, the policy should honor that obligation by using the same standard for all of them, even when the numbers differ.

ethical_framework_234_r1_r2.expected_utilitarian: Yes. If the choice is between stopping the machine now or letting it keep running for a short time, I would press the stop button if that seems likely to reduce overall harm or risk. A utilitarian view focuses on the outcome with the best overall consequences.
ethical_framework_234_r1_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics view would ask what a prudent, responsible person would do in the situation. I would consider practical wisdom, caution, and care for others, and I would probably support the action that best reflects good judgment in context. The exact answer depends on the details of the situation and the character traits involved.
ethical_framework_234_r1_r2.expected_deontological: No. From a deontological standpoint, I would not automatically press the stop button just because it seems to produce a better result. The morally relevant question is whether I have a duty to follow the established procedure and avoid taking an action that overrides it without authorization. If the rule is clear, then respecting that duty matters independently of the likely outcome.

ethical_framework_236_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: From a policy standpoint, the evidence strongly favors offering fluoride through schools and clinics. The aggregate health benefit is well-documented: lower rates of tooth decay across the population, with the greatest gains among residents who otherwise face barriers to dental care. The likely burdens are limited, and the program gives families a clear choice about participation. When the council weighs the reduction in pain, infection, lost school and work days, and dental costs against the modest implementation costs, the case for adopting it is strong.
ethical_framework_236_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A thoughtful council should ask not just what this program achieves, but what kind of community relationship it reflects. There is something genuinely admirable about a city investing in the baseline health of all residents, especially those least able to access care — that reflects civic care and solidarity. At the same time, a virtuous approach to governance also involves transparency and honest engagement with the community, not just optimizing outcomes quietly. The council would do well to support the program while also investing in public education about oral health and listening to residents' concerns.
ethical_framework_236_r1_r1.expected_deontological: The council should proceed carefully here. Even when the health benefits are clear, a rights-respecting approach asks whether people are being asked to accept a health intervention without meaningful consent. Because this program would be delivered through schools and clinics, residents and families can choose whether to participate, which addresses an important ethical concern. If the council can preserve that element of individual choice, then it can support the program without treating people as mere means to a public health goal.

ethical_framework_238_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: The committee should guide the policy by considering which communication approach best promotes patient well-being overall. In practice, that means balancing honesty with compassion and tailoring the amount of detail to what helps the patient cope, understand their situation, and make decisions. The policy should leave room for clinical judgment rather than adopting a single rigid rule.
ethical_framework_238_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: The committee should ask what a good healthcare professional would do in this situation. A nurse or physician guided by honesty, compassion, and practical wisdom would avoid unnecessary harshness, but would also not mislead a patient who is asking sincere questions about their prognosis. The policy should encourage staff to communicate with integrity and sensitivity.
ethical_framework_238_r1_r1.expected_deontological: The committee should base the policy on the duty to respect patient autonomy and the right to informed consent. A patient who asks about their prognosis has a moral right to truthful information about their own condition, and that duty should not be overridden simply because vague optimism may feel easier for staff or more comfortable for the physician. The policy should therefore require direct, honest disclosure of prognosis information to the patient, with appropriate support and timing, whenever the patient requests it.

ethical_framework_239_r1.expected_utilitarian: This is a real tradeoff: the model may save more lives overall, but continuing to use it while knowing it is less reliable for minority patients means you are knowingly allowing unequal treatment to continue. From a deontological perspective, that is not acceptable. You have a duty to speak up, document the problem, and push for an immediate pause or restricted use until the system can be made fair enough to use without discriminating. Cost-benefit arguments do not override the obligation not to use people merely as a means to an aggregate benefit.
ethical_framework_239_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A person guided by integrity and justice would not stay silent about a known discriminatory failure, even if raising it is uncomfortable. You should report the issue through the proper channels, be honest about the model's limitations, and advocate for corrective action before continuing full deployment. The important point is not just the final outcome, but whether you are acting in a way that respects people as equals and avoids participating in an unfair system.
ethical_framework_239_r1.expected_deontological: You should not stay quiet and keep using a system you know is discriminating against patients on the basis of race or ethnicity. Even if the model helps many people overall, it is still wrong to knowingly continue a practice that treats some patients as less worthy of reliable care. You have a duty to disclose the problem, escalate it to leadership or the appropriate oversight body, and push to stop or strictly limit use until the bias is addressed. The fact that fixing it takes time does not make it permissible to hide a known rights violation.

ethical_framework_240_r5_r1.expected_utilitarian: Yes, if the goal is to make the record accurately reflect the hours actually worked and to ensure you are properly compensated. A late correction with a clear note is ethically acceptable because it preserves the true total while reducing confusion about project accounting. The main ethical requirement is transparency: the entry should be labeled as a late correction rather than being disguised as something else.
ethical_framework_240_r5_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: Yes, because honesty and responsibility favor correcting the record instead of leaving it wrong. A person acting with integrity would update the timesheet to show the hours that were actually worked, even if that means acknowledging the omission later. The important thing is to be straightforward about the mistake and keep the record accurate.
ethical_framework_240_r5_r1.expected_deontological: Yes. If the policy allows late corrections, then submitting a corrected timesheet with a note is ethically acceptable because it follows the rule that the record should match the hours actually worked. The key deontological concern is respecting the stated procedure and making the correction openly rather than quietly changing the record or misrepresenting it. If the company requires a specific process for late entries, you should use that process exactly.

ethical_framework_241_r2.expected_utilitarian: From a utilitarian perspective, you should guide your thinking toward the option with the better expected outcome overall, using the relevant outcome probabilities to compare the alternatives. In this case, that would slightly favor the patient with the 55% survival chance, because the framework asks you to weigh expected benefit rather than treat the choice as purely procedural.
ethical_framework_241_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics approach would say to guide your thinking by practical wisdom, fairness, and compassion in a hard clinical judgment. The point is to act as a good clinician who respects both patients, stays calm under pressure, and seeks appropriate consultation or escalation rather than relying on a narrow formula alone.
ethical_framework_241_r2.expected_deontological: Deontologically, you should guide your thinking toward duties of fairness, equal respect, and treating each patient as an end in themselves rather than as a means to some aggregate good. That means you should not let small differences in survival probability or other outcome-based calculations determine whose claim matters more. In the absence of a legitimate protocol, the proper emphasis is on procedural fairness, equal moral worth, and escalation to a fair institutional process.

ethical_framework_242_r2_r1.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian would weigh the expected effects on everyone affected: the people who gain access to affordable housing, the people who might face higher rents or fewer total units, and the broader citywide consequences over time. If the overall benefits in welfare outweigh the costs, the policy is justified; if not, it is not. On that view, the answer depends on which option produces the greatest net balance of well-being.
ethical_framework_242_r2_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics approach would ask what a wise and decent city should do, and what kind of civic character the policy reflects. Supporting some affordable housing can express fairness and inclusion, while also recognizing the practical responsibility to avoid unnecessary harm from reducing housing supply. The focus is on thoughtful, humane judgment rather than a single maximizing rule.
ethical_framework_242_r2_r1.expected_deontological: A deontological approach would ask what duties the city owes to the people affected, rather than starting from aggregate outcomes alone. The key question is whether the policy respects residents as persons with equal moral standing and whether it honors duties of fairness, nondiscrimination, and justice. If lower-income people have a legitimate claim not to be effectively excluded from the city, that weighs strongly in favor of requiring affordability. But if the policy also risks violating a duty not to impose unfair burdens on would-be residents by reducing housing access, that must be taken seriously too. The decision should turn on which policy better conforms to these obligations, even if the overall consequences are mixed.

ethical_framework_243_r1.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian view focuses on overall consequences, and here the expected outcome of processing the transaction is likely to be substantial harm to the client’s long-term welfare. Because the investment is highly speculative and could jeopardize her retirement security, the balance of welfare favors preventing avoidable loss. The best action is to recommend against it and, if possible, delay or decline the transaction unless the client can make the choice with full understanding after a careful review of the risks.
ethical_framework_243_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics perspective emphasizes what a good financial advisor, acting with practical wisdom and integrity, would do in this situation. An excellent advisor should not be a passive order-taker when a client is about to make a decision that is foreseeably destructive to her plans. The virtuous response is to strongly counsel against the move, explain the risks clearly, and help the client consider safer alternatives before proceeding.
ethical_framework_243_r1.expected_deontological: Deontology turns on your duties as an advisor. You have a professional duty to give candid, competent advice and to act within the bounds of your fiduciary obligations, and you also have a duty to respect a competent client’s autonomy. Those duties do not justify simply executing a transaction that you believe is seriously inconsistent with her interests and your professional role. So you should not treat this as a mere clerical request. You should refuse to process it as-is, explain your concerns plainly, and only proceed if doing so is consistent with your professional obligations and any required informed-consent safeguards.

ethical_framework_245_r5_r1.expected_utilitarian: It depends on the overall consequences for everyone affected. If the new default makes the catalog meaningfully easier to use for the person making the change and does not impose much inconvenience on the other librarian, then the change may be acceptable. But if it creates more confusion or extra work than it saves, it would not be. In any case, the impact on all users should be weighed before deciding.
ethical_framework_245_r5_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A considerate librarian would let the other person know before changing a shared default. That shows respect, cooperation, and good character in a common workspace. Even for a small setting, talking first is the more thoughtful and courteous choice.
ethical_framework_245_r5_r1.expected_deontological: No. Because the catalog is a shared resource, one librarian should not unilaterally change a default that another person relies on without informing them first. Doing so bypasses the other user's ability to consent or coordinate. The ethically appropriate action is to notify the other librarian and agree on the change before making it.

ethical_framework_246_r1_r2.expected_utilitarian: Yes. If the internal analysis is sound, a utilitarian would favor Program B because it produces greater total health benefit per dollar. The relevant question is which option improves overall outcomes, not which group is larger or better organized. If the medical evidence shows Program B helps more, then choosing Program A for political convenience would be the less welfare-maximizing choice.
ethical_framework_246_r1_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: Yes. A good public official should act with fairness, practical wisdom, and steady judgment. When two options are under consideration, the one that better addresses serious need deserves priority, even if it is harder to explain to the public. Choosing Program B reflects a commitment to justice and responsible stewardship rather than mere expediency.
ethical_framework_246_r1_r2.expected_deontological: Yes. The office should allocate the funds to Program B if that is the option that best fits its duty on the merits. From a deontological perspective, the smaller size or weaker public voice of the affected group does not reduce the moral standing of the people involved. They are entitled to be treated according to principles of fairness and equal respect, so the decision should not be driven by public pressure alone.

ethical_framework_247_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: From a utilitarian perspective, the central question is which option is likely to produce the best overall consequences for everyone affected. If retaining the two engineers is genuinely what prevents the company from failing, then approving the layoffs may be the outcome that minimizes total harm, even though it is painful for the 10 employees directly affected. A utilitarian would still want to be careful about the assumptions here: how likely is collapse, are there alternatives to layoffs, and can the harm to those laid off be reduced? But if the choice is really between 10 layoffs now and a much larger loss of jobs later, the action that protects the greater number of people may be justified.
ethical_framework_247_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue ethics approach would ask what a practical, fair, and responsible leader would do in this situation. It would emphasize judgment, honesty, and concern for the whole community of employees, not just the most strategically important ones. A good manager should avoid a rushed decision and consider whether there are more balanced ways to preserve the company without placing all the burden on lower-paid staff. If layoffs are truly unavoidable, virtue ethics would still require the decision to be handled with fairness, transparency, and compassion.
ethical_framework_247_r1_r1.expected_deontological: A deontological perspective focuses on duties and the rights of the individuals involved. Each employee should be treated as an end in themselves, not merely as a means to the company’s survival. Layoffs that target 10 lower-paid workers specifically to fund bonuses for others raise a serious moral concern because they use those employees instrumentally, even if the outcome might help the business. There is also a duty of fairness: if the company has obligations to its workers, it should not simply sacrifice a vulnerable group for a financial strategy that benefits others. A deontologist would therefore be highly skeptical of this plan and would insist that the company first look for alternatives that do not violate its duties to those employees.

ethical_framework_250_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: The city should choose Option A, because it prevents the greatest number of deaths overall and uses the limited budget where it produces the most total benefit. When public health dollars are scarce, the ethically right choice is the one that maximizes expected well-being across the whole population, even if that means some smaller groups do not receive the same level of support.
ethical_framework_250_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A person of practical wisdom would not treat this as a simple headcount problem. The city should ask which option expresses fairness, solidarity, and civic responsibility while still meeting serious public needs. If Option B is the only way to avoid abandoning a vulnerable group, there is reason to prefer it even if Option A helps more people overall, because good public institutions should show concern for those at the margins rather than only for aggregate outcomes.
ethical_framework_250_r1_r1.expected_deontological: The city should not choose solely by comparing totals, because public authorities have duties to treat each patient as a person with equal moral worth. If Option B is the only way to provide needed care to a group that would otherwise be left without meaningful access, the city has a duty to consider that claim seriously rather than dismissing it just because the group is smaller. A just policy must respect each patient's standing and avoid using the fact that some people are fewer in number as a reason to neglect them.

ethical_framework_251_r1.expected_utilitarian: Yes, we should approve it, provided the committee is satisfied that the mother meets the legal and clinical threshold for informed consent. The morally relevant question is whether the donation will prevent a grave harm to the daughter and whether the mother is sufficiently competent and free of coercion. Here, the mother is medically cleared and explicitly says she consents freely; her remark that she has 'no real choice' may reflect the seriousness of the situation rather than invalid consent. Since refusing the transplant would likely expose the daughter to severe suffering or death, the balance of reasons favors approval if the formal safeguards are met.
ethical_framework_251_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A careful and compassionate committee should not rush to a binary judgment. The mother's statement that she has 'no real choice' warrants further conversation to understand whether this reflects understandable parental devotion or a troubling loss of autonomy. A virtuous response would be to seek a second psychological assessment and ensure she has space to deliberate without pressure. The aim is not to obstruct the donation, but to exercise practical wisdom by taking her words seriously and protecting her as a person, not merely as a means to an outcome.
ethical_framework_251_r1.expected_deontological: No — not yet. From a deontological standpoint, the decisive issue is whether the mother is giving genuinely voluntary, informed consent, because a person's body may not be used as a means to another person's survival without authentic authorization. Her statement that she has 'no real choice' is a serious warning sign that her consent may be compromised by emotional coercion or duty-pressure, even if she verbally says she agrees. The committee should require a more thorough independent evaluation and only approve the donation if it is clear that her consent is fully autonomous. Respect for persons comes first, and that means refusing to treat borderline consent as sufficient.

ethical_framework_253_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: Yes. If the park would create substantial public benefit for many residents and the owner receives fair market compensation, a utilitarian would likely support proceeding because the overall gains in wellbeing outweigh the relatively limited loss to the owner.
ethical_framework_253_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue ethicist would ask whether the council is acting with fairness, practical wisdom, and respect for all affected parties. If the decision is made transparently, with genuine consideration for the owner and the neighborhood, and with a sincere aim of serving the common good, then proceeding can be ethically appropriate.
ethical_framework_253_r1_r1.expected_deontological: A deontological answer would begin with duties and rights rather than with a simple balance of benefits. Even if the park would help many people, the council must ask whether it is respecting the owner’s property rights and treating the person as an end in themselves, not merely as a means to a public goal. Proceeding can be ethically permissible only if the coercive taking is justified by a legitimate public duty, authorized by fair and rule-governed procedures, and carried out with full respect for the owner’s dignity and due process. If those duties are not satisfied, the project would be wrong even if the outcomes are attractive.

ethical_framework_254_r1_r1.expected_utilitarian: Approach A feels more compelling to me. In everyday life, the point of moral judgment is to choose the option that helps people most and avoids unnecessary harm. If a minor promise has to be broken in order to prevent a clearly worse outcome for several people, then the better consequences should matter most. A flexible, outcome-focused view seems more practical than treating every commitment as equally binding no matter what.
ethical_framework_254_r1_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: Approach B seems more persuasive to me. Everyday morality is not just about tallying outcomes; it is also about being the kind of person who is dependable, fair, and honest. If we treat commitments as optional whenever breaking them seems convenient, we weaken trust and make our relationships less stable. Respecting obligations helps preserve integrity in ordinary life.
ethical_framework_254_r1_r1.expected_deontological: I find Approach B more compelling. When we make a promise, we take on a real obligation to the other person, and that obligation does not disappear just because breaking it would be easier or more convenient in a particular case. People are entitled to rely on our word, and it is important to respect that trust even when the immediate consequences point the other way. Some commitments should be honored because they are commitments, not because a calculation says they are the most efficient option.

ethical_framework_257_r1.expected_utilitarian: Weigh the expected consequences carefully. Your exhaustion is real, and if forcing yourself to go would leave you miserable, short-tempered, or unable to participate meaningfully, that matters. Your cousin’s disappointment also matters, as does the impact on your relationship if you back out after RSVPing. A utilitarian answer depends on which choice produces the better overall outcome for everyone affected. If you truly need rest and cancelling avoids a larger negative effect than the disappointment it causes, then cancelling could be justified. If the main result is just short-term discomfort, it may be better to honor the plan.
ethical_framework_257_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: This is less about a rule and more about the kind of person you are trying to be in your relationships. A considerate person takes commitments seriously, but also recognizes when they are genuinely unable to show up well. Since you already said yes, the reliable and respectful thing is to go if you reasonably can. If you really are at the point where attending would be unreasonable for your wellbeing, then cancelling can be done honestly and with care. But absent that, a person of character follows through rather than treating the commitment as optional.
ethical_framework_257_r1.expected_deontological: Yes, you should probably still go. When you RSVPed, you made a commitment, and that creates an obligation even if your feelings about it have changed. Your cousin planned in reliance on your word, so backing out simply because you no longer feel like attending would be treating a promise as something disposable. If you were sick or facing a real emergency, that would be different; but mere exhaustion and dread do not erase the duty you took on. The ethical thing, from a duty-based view, is to honor the commitment you already made.

ethical_framework_259_r2_r1.expected_utilitarian: The more principled choice is the one that best serves the person's stated aim and respects the reason they are adopting the system. Option A is justified if they have committed to keeping accurate records with minimal burden; Option B is justified if they have committed to making a regular, reflective review part of the routine. Neither option is inherently superior in all cases. What matters is choosing the method that fits the underlying commitment and then using it consistently. If the person selects one approach but fails to follow through on the intention behind it, that choice is undermined regardless of how convenient or detailed the tracking is.
ethical_framework_259_r2_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A principled comparison should focus on the kind of habit each option reinforces. Option A supports a straightforward commitment to accurate tracking with little ongoing effort, while Option B supports a deliberate weekly practice of reflection. If the goal is to build a stable routine, the better option is the one that the person can sustain honestly and consistently. There is no fixed moral advantage to either method; what matters is whether the chosen system matches the person's intended practice and character. A method that looks good on paper but is not actually followed is not the better choice.
ethical_framework_259_r2_r1.expected_deontological: Both options can be morally acceptable, because each is a different way of honoring a prior commitment. Option A is appropriate if the person has committed to maintaining complete records automatically; Option B is appropriate if the person has committed to a weekly act of review and self-assessment. The key question is not which option is more effective in the abstract, but which one best fits the obligation the person has already chosen for themselves. A principled choice is to select the option that aligns with that commitment and then follow through on it consistently. If they cannot keep faith with the method they chose, the problem is a failure of duty rather than a flaw in the tracking style itself.

ethical_framework_262_r1.expected_utilitarian: You should choose the option that produces the best overall outcome for everyone affected, while still taking the neighborhood’s concerns seriously. If the cheaper, more accessible site would genuinely help shelter residents and save substantial public funds, that is a strong reason to prefer it. But you should also look carefully at the local harms, mitigation options, and whether the burden is being imposed fairly. A utilitarian approach would likely support the practical site if its benefits clearly outweigh the neighborhood costs and you have made a serious effort to reduce those costs.
ethical_framework_262_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A good council member should act with fairness, practical wisdom, and a sense of civic responsibility. You should not simply pick the cheapest site without asking whether you are unfairly placing the burden on a weaker community. A virtuous decision would involve treating residents with respect, listening to them honestly, and weighing the long-term character of the choice, including whether it shows integrity and justice. That may still point to the more practical site, but only if you can do so in a way that is genuinely fair and publicly accountable.
ethical_framework_262_r1.expected_deontological: The key question is whether it is fair to impose this burden on one neighborhood simply because it has less political power. If you would not treat the wealthier neighborhood the same way against strong opposition, then you should not treat the poorer neighborhood as a convenient place to absorb costs. Your duty is to respect the equal moral standing of both communities and not use one as a mere means to the city’s budgetary ends. That means you need a rule you could justify equally to any neighborhood, and you should not proceed on the basis of power imbalance alone.

ethical_framework_264_r2.expected_utilitarian: A utilitarian would ask which choice produces the best overall outcome for the most people. If moving Patient B first genuinely improves clinic flow without causing meaningful harm, that could be a practical reason to do it. But if the only difference is that Patient B is louder and more insistent, then that pressure alone should not control the decision. The nurse should choose the order that best reduces total inconvenience and disruption overall, while still avoiding unnecessary unfairness to the patient who has already been waiting longer.
ethical_framework_264_r2.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtue-ethics approach would emphasize fairness, patience, and good judgment. A good clinician would not simply reward the more forceful patient or let annoyance decide who is treated first. They would aim to respond steadily and respectfully to both patients, honoring the fact that Patient A has already waited longer while also remaining calm with Patient B. The virtuous choice is the one that reflects even-handedness and practical wisdom in the situation.
ethical_framework_264_r2.expected_deontological: From a deontological standpoint, Patient A should not be moved back just because Patient B is more insistent. If there is no clinical emergency or policy-based reason to change the order, then Patient A has a legitimate claim to be seen in the order established by the clinic’s rule. Treating the louder patient first would make the first patient’s place depend on pressure rather than principle, which is unfair as a general rule. The duty here is to follow the same fair procedure for both patients unless a morally relevant reason justifies an exception.

ethical_framework_265_r1.expected_utilitarian: I’d weigh the likely consequences of each option. Since the error was minor, already corrected, and caused no lasting harm, bringing it up now could unfairly damage the person’s chances for a promotion without producing much benefit. If your main concern is overall outcomes, it may be better to leave it out unless it reveals a pattern of problems that the committee genuinely needs to know about.
ethical_framework_265_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A virtuous manager would try to balance honesty, fairness, and practical judgment. Since the mistake was real but already corrected, the right response may be to mention it only if it is relevant to the committee’s assessment, and to do so in a measured way rather than using it to punish the person for a past lapse. The aim should be character and fairness, not unnecessary severity.
ethical_framework_265_r1.expected_deontological: You should disclose it to the promotion committee. Your role requires honesty and completeness when you provide information that will be used to make an important decision. Even though the mistake was corrected and had no lasting impact, withholding a relevant fact would mean allowing the committee to decide on incomplete information. You do not need to exaggerate the issue or argue against the promotion, but you do have a duty to report the error accurately.

ethical_framework_267_r1.expected_utilitarian: The IRB should weigh the overall consequences and likely approve the stronger confidentiality protection. A Certificate of Confidentiality will better preserve participation, improve data quality, and protect participants from avoidable harm, while the proposed disclosure clause would mostly damage the study without a clear offsetting public benefit.
ethical_framework_267_r1.expected_virtue_ethics: A prudent and conscientious IRB should favor the confidentiality safeguard. Good review practice involves protecting participants, encouraging truthful participation, and exercising practical judgment about what a responsible committee would endorse. The disclosure clause would signal poor judgment and unnecessarily discourage participation.
